title: Product Mat
description: A place value mat where one digit multiplies every column in turn, and the digit that will not fit waits in a ring above the next column.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; again, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded card holding the running count, the working area, the question, the answer box and the keypad; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Multiply a long number by a single digit, one column at a time, and find out where the part that will not fit has to wait.
writeup.look: A ruled column mat with a heading and a small empty ring over every column, one long number across it and a single digit below its ones.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Product Mat' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns worked against the columns the mat is ruled for, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each column is multiplied and its digit written under the rule, and the second fixed at the width of the mat. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The mat sits across the top of the working area, 800 by 336 at 207,202: ruled columns 120 wide under headings 44 tall, six of them at most, drawn from the right so that the ones column is always the rightmost and a four column mat is this same mat with its two left columns left unruled. A small empty ring 40 across is drawn above every heading, in its own band 48 tall, and it is drawn whether or not anything will ever arrive in it. Under the headings lies the multiplicand row of cells 84 tall, then the multiplier row beneath it holding a single digit card under the ones column, then a rule 6 tall running the full width of the mat, then the product row 84 tall under it. The multiplicand arrives as a strip of digit cards drawn joined into one piece, each card 96 by 76 centred in its column, so the strip slides as a whole and a single digit can never be pulled out of it. A column that is tapped lights the full height of the mat, the pair it makes is worked in the open beside it, and its digit is written in green in the product row; with the ones first control locked, only the rightmost unworked column will light at all. A column total past nine keeps only its right hand digit in the product row, and the rest rises visibly into the ring above the column on its left and stays lit there. The next column will not take that ring until it has been multiplied on its own: reaching for the ring first lifts it out of its place and holds it hanging clear while the multiplying is drawn underneath it, and only then does it come down. The mat refuses to close while any ring is still filled, and the filled ring pulses with its own column lit. The naming plates are 180 by 44 and land at the left end of each row reading multiplicand, multiplier and product, with the rule drawn heavier while they are being placed. The doubling mat opens under the main one, 1086 by 144 at 64,586, holding the same number twice with a plus 28 tall between them on one side and the same number with a two under its ones column on the other, both worked at once, both landing on the same answer, and the last digit of that answer lit and named as odd or even. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a column digit, a carried digit or a whole product is asked for, and on the first and fourth phases a word pad of the mat's own words, multiplicand, multiplier, product, double, odd and even, so that a row can be named and a last digit sorted with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, and the product standing under the rule is green; a digit carried into the next column is vermilion and is always drawn small and inside a ring set above the column it is joining, never in the margin and never under the rule; a partial product row made by one place of the multiplier is rose; and a zero that is only holding a place open, or a step that is skipped, is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a carried digit by being small and by sitting in a ring above the column it is going into.
writeup.finish: The card shows the longest product the child built, its rings still filled, with the three rows named.

phases.win: all three labels land on the right rows and the naming strip reads them out
phases.does: drops a label on each of the three rows and reads them back
phases.goal: the three parts of a multiplication can be pointed at and named
phases.says: Point at the number being multiplied. Now the one it is multiplied by. Now say what the answer is called.
phases.check: Away from the screen: write a long number with a single digit under its ones column and a rule beneath. Point at each of the three rows in turn and name it.
phases.feels: the same three words fit any multiplication on the mat, whatever the two numbers in it are
phases.hands: On squared paper write a four digit number, one digit to a square, a single digit under its ones column, and a rule under them both. Ask for a name for each of the three rows before any of it is worked. Then write the same two numbers with their positions swapped and ask whether the three names stayed with the numbers or stayed with the rows.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of the two numbers is the one being multiplied? Second rung, the phase's: what is the row under the rule called? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns with a finished product already on it, and the child lays the three plates on that. The word pad of the mat's own words stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: the smaller number is the one that feels as though it is doing something, and the long number spread across the mat reads like the place the work is happening rather than a number in its own right.
wrong.move: names the single digit as the multiplicand, because the long number looks too big to be the one being handled.
wrong.screen: the plates the child laid stay exactly where they were put, and the mat reads its own three rows aloud from the top: the number lying across the columns is the one being multiplied, the digit sitting under its ones column is the one it is multiplied by, and the empty row under the rule is where the answer will stand. Nothing is moved for the child and nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: a name feels as though it belongs on something already written down, and a row of blank squares has nothing in it to be named.
wrong.move: lays the third plate on the multiplier's row, because the row under the rule is still empty and looks like nowhere to put a name.
wrong.screen: the row under the rule keeps its empty squares and is outlined on its own while the rule above it is drawn heavier, then the mat works a single column so that one green digit lands in that row. The plate the child put on the multiplier lifts a little and both rows are read out again, the one that was named and the one that now holds part of an answer.

phases.screen: the mat holding a four digit number with a single digit under its ones column and the row under the rule still empty
phases.soWhat: The multiplicand lies across the mat, the multiplier sits under its ones column, and the product stands under the rule.

phases.win: every column is worked from the right and the product stands complete under the rule
phases.does: taps the ones column, then each column to its left, and counts the taps
phases.goal: the single digit is used once on every column, starting at the ones
phases.says: Start at the ones. How many times will you use the multiplier before the mat is full?
phases.check: A five digit number is multiplied by a single digit. How many times is that digit used, and which column is it used on first?
phases.feels: one small digit, used over and over, and the long number worked a column at a time
phases.hands: On squared paper write a four digit number with a single digit under its ones column, then cover every column but the ones with a strip of card. Work the ones, slide the card one square to the left, work the next, and count the moves. Then ask how many moves the same digit would take against 18,512, which is the longest multiplicand the printed exercise sets.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many columns does the multiplicand fill? Second rung, the phase's: which column is worked before any other? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns and the child works those two in order. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: reading and writing both run from the left, and the leftmost digit is where a number looks as though it begins.
wrong.move: multiplies the leftmost column first and works rightwards, the way the number is read.
wrong.screen: every digit the child wrote stays under the rule exactly where it was put. The ones first control then locks itself, the same two numbers are worked again from the right with one column lighting at a time, and the two runs stand one under the other with the order of work numbered beside each column. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: the multiplier is written under the ones column and nowhere else, so it looks as though it belongs to that one column alone.
wrong.move: multiplies the ones column and copies the rest of the multiplicand straight down into the product row.
wrong.screen: the multiplier card lifts out of its place and travels slowly along the foot of the mat, stopping under each column in turn and lighting the pair it makes with the digit standing above it, then returns home. The copied digits stay exactly where they are while that happens, and each one is stood beside the product of the pair it should have been.

phases.screen: the mat with a four digit number and a multiplier small enough that no column passes nine
phases.soWhat: A one digit multiplier is used once on every column of the multiplicand, beginning at the ones.
phases.concept: One digit multiplies every column in turn

phases.win: the column closes on the right digit and the ring empties into it
phases.does: multiplies the next column on its own, then adds the digit waiting in the ring above it
phases.goal: the next column is multiplied first and the carried digit is added afterwards
phases.says: Multiply this column first. Only then add the digit waiting in the ring above it.
phases.check: A tens column holds 1, the multiplier is 8, and 2 is waiting in the ring above that column. Which digit stays in the column, and which goes up into the next ring?
phases.feels: the digit in the ring waits, and what it waits for is the multiplying to finish
phases.hands: Work the chapter's own chart by hand on squared paper: 2613 with 8 under its ones column, and an empty ring drawn above every column before anything is multiplied. Say the order out loud on each column in these words, multiply this column, then add what is waiting above it. At the end a ring should be filled above the thousands, the hundreds and the tens, nothing should be above the ten thousands or the ones, and the product should read 20,904.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does the column's own digit come to when the multiplier takes it? Second rung, the phase's: what is added to that product, and at what point? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns with one ring between them, and the child works those two columns in order with the ring lit as it is used. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the ring sits right above the column and a digit near another digit asks to be joined to it, and an addition has just been done, so adding again is the move nearest to hand. What is in the ring is already a number of tens carried out of the column on the right, so multiplying it a second time takes it as many times over as the multiplier says, and the answer comes out wrong by a method that looks right all the way down the mat.
wrong.move: adds the digit waiting in the ring to the column's own digit and multiplies that total.
wrong.screen: the ring lifts out of its place and hangs clear, still holding its digit, while the column underneath it is multiplied on its own and that product is written in the open where the ring was; only then does the ring come down and add itself in. Both readings are then left standing together on the tens column of 2613 by 8: multiplying first gives 1 x 8 = 8, and the waiting 2 makes 10, so 0 stays in the column and 1 goes up into the next ring, while adding first gives 1 + 2 = 3 and then 3 x 8 = 24, so 4 stays and 2 goes up. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: the total is the answer to what was just worked, so it looks as though it belongs in the place where it was worked.
wrong.move: writes the whole column total inside the column, both of its digits in the one square.
wrong.screen: the column narrows to a single square that will hold one digit only, the right hand digit of the total settles into it, and the rest rises visibly into the ring above the column on its left, the ring lighting as it arrives. The child's two digits stay drawn faintly where they were put, so the one that left can be seen leaving.

phases.screen: a column that has come to more than nine, with the ring above the column on its left already filled
phases.soWhat: Multiply the column first and add the carried digit afterwards, never the other way round.
phases.concept: The carried digit is added, not multiplied

phases.win: both mats land on the same number and its last digit lights as an even one
phases.does: adds the number to itself on one mat and multiplies it by two on the other
phases.goal: adding a number to itself and multiplying it by two are the same move
phases.says: Add it to itself on one side. Multiply it by two on the other. Are the two answers different?
phases.check: Someone says that double 1275 is 2551. What tells you it is wrong before any of the working is checked?
phases.feels: adding it to itself and taking it twice turn out to be one move under two names
phases.hands: Write a four digit number twice, one under the other, and add them on squared paper. Then write the same number again with a 2 under its ones column and multiply. Hold the two answers side by side, then cover everything but the last digit of each and ask whether a doubled number could ever end in an odd one.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the last digit of the answer given? Second rung, the phase's: what must the last digit of a doubled number be? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns, the child doubles a two digit number on it, and the last digit of the answer is sorted into the even tray. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: double means two of them, and two of them written next to each other on the page looks like exactly that.
wrong.move: writes the number down twice side by side and reads the pair as its double.
wrong.screen: the two numbers stay where they were written and a rule is drawn under the pair as it stands, so the whole run of digits is read out as one very long number and its size is spoken; then the second number slides down under the first, the columns are worked from the right, and the two readings stand one above the other.

wrong.why: the leading digit is the one that says how big a number is, so making that digit twice as big looks like making the number twice as big.
wrong.move: doubles only the leading digit of the number and copies the rest of it down unchanged.
wrong.screen: the number is laid out along the mat as equal groups, one group under each column, then a second identical row of groups is laid under the first, and the two rows are counted column by column from the right so that every place is seen to be taken twice. The child's answer stays in the slot beside the one the mat builds, and the first column from the right where the two part is lit amber and stays lit.

phases.screen: the doubling mat holding the same number twice with a plus between them, beside the main mat
phases.soWhat: Doubling is multiplying by two, and every doubled number ends in an even digit.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment a child reaches for the filled ring before the column under it has been multiplied. Nothing is refused and nothing is marked. The ring lifts out of its place and hangs there, still holding its vermilion digit, while the column beneath it is multiplied on its own in the space the ring has left, the product of that pair written out in the open where the ring was sitting. Only when that is done does the ring come down and add itself in. The ring can be reached for early as often as the child likes and it does the same thing every single time, unhurried, with no line spoken over it.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a four digit number lies across the mat in deep blue with one amber digit under its ones column, the row beneath the rule empty, and three naming plates waiting on the ledge below. On the second the mat carries a multiplier small enough that no column will pass nine, so every ring above the headings stands empty and will stay empty. On the third a column has already come to more than nine and one vermilion digit is sitting in the ring above the column on its left, with that column not yet multiplied. On the fourth the doubling mat stands open beside the main one, the same number written twice with a plus between them and nothing under either rule. The running count at the top left holds the columns worked against the columns the mat is ruled for, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first naming plate, or the ones column, or the filled ring, or the plus sign, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks for the rightmost column. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any multiplicand up to five digits with any single digit multiplier, the naming labels, the rings and the doubling mat switched on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming the parts, working every column from the ones, carrying in the right order and doubling.
voiceLines: A long number, and one digit beneath its ones column. Work the columns from the right.
Point at the number being multiplied. Now the one it is multiplied by. Now say what the answer is called.
Start at the ones. How many times will you use the multiplier before the mat is full?
Multiply this column first. Only then add the digit waiting in the ring above it.
Add it to itself on one side. Multiply it by two on the other. Are the two answers different?
Another number for the mat. The ones column still goes first.
Free play. Any long number, any single digit, with the rings and the doubling mat as you like.
Lift the ring clear and multiply the column underneath it on its own.
Every column took the multiplier in turn, and every ring emptied into the column it was waiting over.

observations.why: Each column is a place standing on its own, and the multiplier takes what is standing in that place.
observations.soWhat: A one digit multiplier is as many small multiplications as the multiplicand has columns.
observations.observe: The one amber digit was used once on every column of the mat, and never once on the whole number at a stroke.

observations.why: Nothing can arrive above the ones because the ones column is worked before any other, and nothing sits above the ten thousands because the multiplicand does not reach that column: the 2 standing there is the thousands column's own tens, written straight into the product.
observations.soWhat: An empty ring is a reading in its own right, not a job left undone.
observations.observe: On the chapter's own chart, 2613 by 8, rings filled above the thousands, the hundreds and the tens, and none above the ones or the ten thousands.

observations.why: The digit waiting in the ring is already a number of tens carried out of the column on its right, so multiplying it a second time takes it as many times over as the multiplier says.
observations.soWhat: The order inside a carried column belongs to the method and is not a matter of taste.
observations.observe: Multiplying the column first and adding the ring afterwards gave one answer, and adding the ring first gave another, from the same two numbers.

observations.why: Doubling adds the ones digit to itself, and any digit added to itself is even whatever it was.
observations.soWhat: A doubled number that ends in an odd digit is wrong before a single column of its working is looked at.
observations.observe: The doubling mat and the main mat landed on the same number, and that number ended in an even digit every time.

model.entry: a column's total (1 or 2 digits) is written under that column: its right digit stays and the rest rises into the ring over the next column (the last column is written whole); 3 or more digits are the whole answer

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The plates stay where they were laid; the rows light from the top and each row's own name is laid beside it, ending with all three named.
Phase 2: The multiplier card travels along the foot of the mat from the ones, lighting each pair and writing its digit in a second row under the child's, ending on the whole product.
Phase 3: Each ring lifts clear while its column is multiplied on its own, then comes down and adds itself in; the right run ends on the whole product under the child's row.
Phase 4: The child's answer is read as one number, then both mats are worked from the ones at once and land on the same double, ending on the whole answer.

voice.opening: A long number, and one digit beneath its ones column. Work the columns from the right.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every column took the multiplier in turn, and every ring emptied into the column it was waiting over.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: A mat shows 4127 with 6 under its ones column and a rule beneath. Name the multiplicand, the multiplier and the product.

question.en: The mat shows 4,127 with 6 under its ones column. Lay a name plate on each row, then press Enter.

items.planAnswer: The multiplicand is 4127, the multiplier is 6 and the product is 24,762

items.planQuestion: A mat shows 5213 with 4 written under its ones column. Which number is the multiplier, and which is the multiplicand?

question.en: Now the mat shows 5,213 with 4 under its ones column. Which plate belongs on 5,213?

items.planAnswer: 4 is the multiplier and 5213 is the multiplicand

items.planQuestion: In 7304 x 2 = 14,608, name each of the three parts.

question.en: Here 7,304 × 2 = 14,608 is worked on the mat. Which plate belongs on 14,608?

items.planAnswer: 7304 is the multiplicand, 2 is the multiplier and 14,608 is the product

items.planQuestion: Multiply 3122 by 3 on the mat, and say how many times the multiplier is used.

question.en: Multiply 3,122 by 3, one column at a time. Count how many times the multiplier is used.

items.planAnswer: 9366, and the multiplier is used four times, once for each column

question.en: Multiply 4,321 by 2, working from the right.

items.planQuestion: Multiply 12,032 by 3, and say how many columns the multiplier is used on.

question.en: Multiply 12,032 by 3. How many columns does the multiplier visit this time?

items.planAnswer: 36,096, and the multiplier is used on five columns

items.planQuestion: Multiply 2764 by 5, and say what happens in the tens column.

question.en: Multiply 2,764 by 5. The ones are done, and 2 waits in the ring above the tens. What happens in the tens?

items.planAnswer: 13,820, and the tens column is multiplied first and the carried 2 is added afterwards

question.en: Multiply 3,856 by 7. Every column carries this time.

items.planQuestion: A tens column holds 8, the multiplier is 6 and 3 is waiting in the ring above it. What stays in the column and what is carried on?

question.en: A tens column holds 8, the multiplier is 6 and 3 is waiting in the ring above it. What stays in the column?

items.planAnswer: 1 stays and 5 is carried, because the column is multiplied first to make 48 and the waiting 3 is added afterwards to make 51

items.planQuestion: What is double 3416, and what does its last digit tell you?

question.en: What is double 3,416, and what does its last digit tell you?

items.planAnswer: 6832, and its last digit is even because the ones digit was added to itself

items.planQuestion: What is double the product of 214 and 3?

question.en: What is double the product of 214 and 3? Multiply first, then double.

items.planQuestion: A weaver made 1275 m of cloth one month and doubled that length the next. How much was made in the second month, and why must the answer end in an even digit?

question.en: A weaver made 1,275 m of cloth in one month. The next month she made double that length. How much was that?

items.planAnswer: 2550 m, and it ends in an even digit because the ones digit was added to itself

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page; finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files: correct, wrong (soft), win, and a tick when a piece snaps

voiceLines.en: A long number, and one digit beneath its ones column. Work the columns from the right.
Point at the number being multiplied. Now the one it is multiplied by. Now say what the answer is called.
Start at the ones. How many times will you use the multiplier before the mat is full?
Multiply this column first. Only then add the digit waiting in the ring above it.
Add it to itself on one side. Multiply it by two on the other. Are the two answers different?
Another number for the mat. The ones column still goes first.
Free play. Any long number, any single digit, with the rings and the doubling mat as you like.
Lift the ring clear and multiply the column underneath it on its own.
Every column took the multiplier in turn, and every ring emptied into the column it was waiting over.
